title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about prompting AI to learn, at an advanced level. Not what AI is, and not basic use, but how you drive it skilfully so it deepens your understanding rather than replaces it. By the end you will be able to build strong prompts, deepen a dialogue with deliberate moves, and use techniques that make you do the thinking.

These are practical skills you can use this week, in any subject. They build on honest, critical AI use: prompting well is how you get real value from a tool while staying the one who thinks.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: construct effective learning prompts using a role, a function and context
combine prompt moves to deepen an AI dialogue instead of starting over
design AI techniques that build your own understanding rather than replace it.

title: In real academic practice
body: Prompting well applies to the work you are already doing. Every explanation you ask for, every answer you push deeper, and every technique you use to test your understanding draws on skills that study and work both reward. Build them now and they carry into every module, and into professional work where these tools are already part of the day.

title: Signpost
body: The course has four short lessons. First, the prompt framework: building a prompt from a role, a function and context. Second, prompt moves: deepening a dialogue instead of restarting. Third, techniques that build understanding: eight ways to learn with AI. Fourth, designing your own routine that joins all three. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: You already know what generative AI can do and have used it on study tasks. This lesson takes up the skill that makes it genuinely useful: writing the prompt. A good prompt does not just fetch an answer - it makes the tool work on your problem, and makes you think first.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to build prompts on purpose, not type whatever comes to mind. You should be able to name the parts of a strong prompt, say why each one matters, and defend the prompt you wrote as the one most likely to help you learn.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: construct a learning prompt from a role, a function and context
combine the prompt habits that make a tool think with you, not for you
construct a prompt for a task in {{context}} and justify why it will produce a useful answer.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A strong learning prompt has three parts. The role tells the tool who to be, such as a supportive tutor or a tough examiner. The function is the exact task: explain, compare, quiz, or critique. The context is what you bring: your level, your module, what you have covered, and the terms you find hard.

Two habits make these parts work harder. Ask for the method and the reasoning, not just the finished answer, so you can follow and check it. And invite nuance: ask what is usually oversimplified, or where experts disagree. A prompt built this way makes you think first, and even one line of your own attempt improves what comes back.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last prompt you wrote for your studies. Did it give the tool a role, a function and your context? Rewrite it now as a stronger prompt.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A strong prompt is built, not blurted: a role, a clear function and your own context, with a request for the method rather than the finished answer. You can now construct a prompt from those three parts, combine the habits that make a tool think with you, and build a prompt for your own work that you can justify. Next, you will learn the moves that turn one prompt into a productive dialogue.

title: Orientation
body: One prompt rarely gets you all the way. The first answer from a tool is usually broad and a little flat. This lesson is about what you do next: the moves that turn a weak first answer into something genuinely useful, without starting over.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to treat prompting as a dialogue you steer. You should be able to choose a move that fits the gap in an answer, sequence several moves so each builds on the last, and say why that sequence deepens the work rather than resetting it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: combine prompt moves to enrich an answer without starting over
design a sequence of moves that deepens a dialogue rather than resets it
choose the prompt moves that will strengthen an answer for a task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A prompt move is a follow-up that improves the answer you already have. Five moves do most of the work. Expand asks for more, such as counter-arguments to each point. Add context feeds in your module, examples or constraints. Go deeper asks the tool to compare, elaborate or explain the reasoning. Check bias asks what viewpoints are missing. Verify asks what you should fact-check and which sources to find.

The point is that prompting is iterative, not a single exchange. Each move keeps the dialogue you have built and sharpens it. Starting a fresh prompt throws that progress away and usually returns another flat, general answer.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a recent AI dialogue that disappointed you. Which move - expand, add context, go deeper, check bias or verify - would have helped most? Why?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Prompting is a dialogue, not a single exchange. When the first answer falls short, you make a move - expand, add context, go deeper, check bias, or verify - rather than start over. You can now combine these moves to enrich an answer, design a sequence that deepens rather than resets, and choose the moves that fit your own task. Next come the techniques that turn these moves into real understanding.

title: Orientation
body: A good prompt and the right moves get you a useful answer. The deeper question is whether you end up understanding anything. This lesson covers eight techniques that use AI to build your own understanding, so the thinking stays yours rather than the tool's.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to use AI to learn, not to be told. You should be able to pick the technique that fits what you want to understand, use it so you do the thinking, and judge afterwards whether your understanding actually grew.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: match the eight techniques to the kind of understanding each one builds
combine techniques so you do the thinking and the tool supports it
design a short study routine in {{context}} using the techniques that fit.

title: Concept: definition
body:
These techniques share one principle: use AI as a partner, not an answer machine. You do the thinking; the tool prompts, questions and checks. That is what turns information on a screen into understanding you keep.

The eight run from explaining an idea back in your own words, through being questioned, practising, getting feedback on your work, mapping how ideas connect, arguing against your own position, learning through analogy, and preparing for hard reading. Each is a different way to make yourself work. The activity below sets out what each one is and a prompt to start it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of an idea in your studies you find hard. Which of these eight techniques would help you understand it, and what prompt would you use to start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Deep learning comes from doing the work, with the tool as a partner. Explaining back, Socratic questioning, practice and feedback, feedback on your work, mapping, devil's advocate, analogy and reading preparation all share one move: you think, and the tool helps. You can now match a technique to what you want to learn and build a short routine from them. The last lesson brings the framework, the moves and the techniques together.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Build a learning prompt
body: A strong learning prompt names who the AI should be, what it should do, and your own context. Build one below, then copy it and try it in a real AI tool.
instruction: Pick a chip, choose from the list, or type your own in each part.
_assembleTemplate: Act as {role}. {function}. Context: my level is {level}, I am working on {module}, and I find {difficulty} hard.
_whyText: A role, a clear task and your own context make the answer specific - and asking for the method, not the answer, keeps the thinking yours.

_parts.label: Role
_parts.help: What should the AI act as?
_chips: a supportive tutor for a first-year
a critical friend who challenges my reasoning
an expert examiner in my field

_parts.label: Function
_chips: explain the method step by step, not just the answer
give me a structural checklist, do not write it for me
quiz me, then tell me what I misunderstood

_parts.label: Module or topic
_parts.help: The module or topic you are working on.
_parts.placeholder: e.g. the topic you are revising

_parts.label: What you find hard
_parts.help: The specific thing you are stuck on.
_parts.placeholder: e.g. telling two key terms apart

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Prompts you can adapt
body: Keep a few reliable prompts to hand. Open each group and change the wording to fit your own topic.
instruction: Select each heading to open it.

_items.title: Understand and explain
_items.body: Meet a new idea. 'Explain this concept as if I am new to the subject.' Or: 'Explain it three ways, simple, intermediate and advanced.'

_items.title: Test yourself
_items.body: Practise recall. 'Quiz me on this topic and give feedback on my answers.' Or: 'What questions should I be able to answer about this?'

_items.title: Improve your thinking
_items.body: Find the gaps. 'What mistakes do students often make with this concept?' Or: 'Here is my understanding. What is missing or wrong?'

_items.title: Enrich a thin answer
_items.body: Push a general reply further. 'Give counter-arguments for each point.' Or: 'Compare two theories and say when each is more useful.'

_items.title: Check before you trust it
_items.body: Pressure-test the output. 'What viewpoints are underrepresented here?' Or: 'List what I should fact-check, and suggest academic keywords to search.'

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students want help revising research methods, and each writes one prompt for the same AI tool.

{{learner-a}} types a single line: explain research methods. The answer is long, generic, and pitched at no particular level. It never mentions {{learner-a}}'s module, it muddles the very terms {{learner-a}} finds hard, and it offers nothing to practise. {{learner-a}} reads it, feels no clearer, and has done no real thinking.

{{learner-b}} builds the prompt in three parts. The role is a supportive tutor for a first-year. The function is to explain the difference between qualitative and quantitative methods, then set five short questions and hide the answers. The context is a social sciences student who keeps confusing methods with methodology. The reply is pitched right, names the trap, and gives {{learner-b}} something to attempt.

Both asked about the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} gave the tool a role, a function and a context, and so got an answer that made them think.

title: Building a strong prompt
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These checks turn a vague request into a prompt that makes the tool work and makes you think. Try them on your next AI-assisted task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I told the tool a role to play?
Have I named one clear function, the exact task I want?
Have I given my context: level, module and the terms I find hard?
Have I asked for the method and reasoning, not just the answer?
Have I invited nuance, such as what is oversimplified or contested?
Have I put down my own first attempt before asking?

title: Formative check: the three parts
displayTitle: Which prompt is most likely to get a useful, learning-focused answer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which prompt is most likely to get a useful, learning-focused answer?

_items.text: Act as a tutor for a first-year; explain the method step by step and then quiz me; I confuse two key terms.
_items.feedback: Yes. It sets a role, a clear function and your context, and asks for the method.

_items.text: Tell me everything about this topic.
_items.feedback: Too broad: no role, no specific task and no context, so the answer stays generic.

_items.text: Write the answer for me so I can hand it in.
_items.feedback: That asks the tool to do the work, not to help you learn or think.

_items.text: Give me a confident, polished paragraph on this topic.
_items.feedback: Polish is not understanding; this asks for fluency, not the method you can follow.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A role, a clear function and your context, plus a request for the method, make a learning prompt.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option with a role, a specific task and your own context.
_incorrect.final: The strong prompt names a role, a clear function and your context, and asks for the method. Breadth, hand-in answers or polish do not.

title: Formative check: why it works
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second prompt produce a more useful answer than the first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second prompt produce a more useful answer than the first?

_items.text: It gave the tool a role, a specific function and the student's own context.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those three parts make the answer specific and push you to think.

_items.text: It was written in more formal and confident language.
_items.feedback: Formality is not the point; the three parts are.

_items.text: It asked the tool for a longer answer.
_items.feedback: Length does not make an answer useful.

_items.text: It used the exact wording from the module handbook.
_items.feedback: Borrowed wording is not what made the difference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A role, a clear function and real context make the answer specific.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second prompt added that the first left out.
_incorrect.final: The second prompt supplied a role, a function and the student's context. Tone, length and borrowed wording were not the difference.

title: Formative check: your own task
displayTitle: You want help with a task in {{context}}. Which prompt best uses the framework?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which prompt best uses the framework for a task in your subject?

_items.text: Act as a tutor in {{context}}; explain the method for this task, then set me questions; here is my level and the part I find hard.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a role, a function and your context give the tool what it needs.

_items.text: Ask the tool to complete the task in {{context}} and return a finished answer.
_items.feedback: That asks the tool to do the task, not to help you learn it.

_items.text: Type the task title from {{context}} and nothing else.
_items.feedback: With no role, function or context, the answer stays generic.

_items.text: Ask for the most confident-sounding answer about {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Confidence is not usefulness; you still need the method and your context.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you set a role, a clear function and your own context, and ask for the method.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the prompt that gives a role, a function and your context in {{context}}.
_incorrect.final: A strong prompt in {{context}} names a role, a function and your context, and asks for the method. A bare title, a hand-in request, or a demand for confidence do not.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Five moves that deepen a dialogue
body: Five follow-up moves that improve an answer without starting over. Review each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Expand
_items.subtitle: Ask for more
_items.text: Ask the tool to widen the answer, for example by giving a counter-argument for each point it made.

_items.title: Add context
_items.subtitle: Bring your module in
_items.text: Feed in your level, your module or a constraint, so the next answer fits your actual task.

_items.title: Go deeper
_items.subtitle: Reasoning, not just claims
_items.text: Ask the tool to compare two ideas, elaborate a point, or show the reasoning behind a claim.

_items.title: Check bias
_items.subtitle: What is missing
_items.text: Ask which viewpoints are underrepresented, or what the answer quietly leaves out.

_items.title: Verify
_items.subtitle: Make it checkable
_items.text: Ask what you should fact-check and which academic sources would confirm or challenge the answer.

title: Spot the line
displayTitle: Sharpen your prompt
body: Small changes turn a flat prompt into one that builds real understanding. Flip each card to see a weak prompt become a learning prompt.
instruction: Select a card to flip it.

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'How does photosynthesis work, and why does it matter for ecosystems?'

A why-and-how question moves you past a definition into real understanding.

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'How does this idea connect to the other topics from this week?'

Linking ideas helps them stick and shows how a subject fits together.

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'Here is my explanation. What have I misunderstood or oversimplified?'

Sharing your thinking first turns AI into a checker, not a source.

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'What should I explore next, and what does this imply?'

Planned follow-up keeps the dialogue going instead of stopping at the first answer.

front.title: Ask for the method
front.body: Weak prompt: 'Give me the final answer.'

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'Show me the steps someone would use, and explain why each one matters.'

A method you can follow teaches more than an answer you could copy.

back.title: Sharper
back.body:
'What is commonly oversimplified here, and where do experts still disagree?'

Asking for nuance takes you beyond a textbook answer.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students each get a bland first answer from an AI tool about a theory they are studying.

{{learner-a}} is not satisfied, so {{learner-a}} deletes the chat and writes a brand-new prompt from scratch. The second answer is just as general as the first. {{learner-a}} tries a third time, rewording the question again, and keeps losing the thread. Nothing builds, because every attempt starts over.

{{learner-b}} keeps the dialogue going. First {{learner-b}} asks the tool to go deeper and compare two versions of the theory. Then {{learner-b}} adds context: use examples from my module. Next {{learner-b}} asks what the answer leaves out, and finally asks which claims to verify against the reading. Each move sharpens the last, and the answer becomes genuinely useful.

Both started from the same weak answer. Only {{learner-b}} improved it with deliberate moves instead of starting again.

title: Making prompt moves
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn a flat first answer into something useful, without restarting. Try them on your next AI dialogue.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I keep the dialogue going rather than start a new prompt?
Did I expand the answer where it was thin?
Did I add context from my module or task?
Did I go deeper, asking for comparison or reasoning?
Did I check what viewpoints or caveats were missing?
Did I ask what to verify and which sources to find?

title: Formative check: the next move
displayTitle: A tool's first answer is clear but too general. What is the best next move?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A tool's first answer is too general. What is the best next move?

_items.text: Make a move on the same answer, such as adding context or asking it to go deeper.
_items.feedback: Yes. A move builds on what you have rather than throwing it away.

_items.text: Delete the chat and write a completely new prompt.
_items.feedback: Starting over loses the dialogue and usually returns another general answer.

_items.text: Accept the answer and move on.
_items.feedback: A general answer left as is does little for your learning.

_items.text: Ask the same question again in different words.
_items.feedback: Rewording from scratch is not a move; it resets the dialogue.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Making a move deepens the answer you already have.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that builds on the first answer.
_incorrect.final: The best next move builds on the answer you have, such as adding context or going deeper. Restarting, accepting or rewording do not.

title: Formative check: building vs restarting
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student's answer end up more useful than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student's answer end up more useful?

_items.text: They improved the first answer with deliberate moves instead of starting a new prompt each time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Moves build on the dialogue; restarting throws it away.

_items.text: They used a more powerful AI tool for the task.
_items.feedback: The tool was the same; the difference was how they used it.

_items.text: They accepted the first answer and moved on quickly.
_items.feedback: Accepting a flat answer is what the first student did.

_items.text: They asked the same question in three slightly different ways.
_items.feedback: Rewording from scratch resets the dialogue; it is not a move.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Deliberate moves on one dialogue build on what came before.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student did with the first answer.
_incorrect.final: The second student made deliberate moves on one dialogue - deeper, more context, checking and verifying. A different tool, quick acceptance or rewording were not the point.

title: Formative check: your own task
displayTitle: On a task in {{context}}, a tool gives a thin first answer. Which move best strengthens it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best strengthens a thin answer for a task in your subject?

_items.text: Add context from {{context}} and ask the tool to go deeper on the key comparison.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, adding context and depth builds on the answer you have.

_items.text: Start again with a new prompt about {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Restarting loses the dialogue and usually returns another thin answer.

_items.text: Accept the answer because it sounds like {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Sounding right is not being useful; the answer is still thin.

_items.text: Ask for a longer version of the same answer.
_items.feedback: Length alone does not deepen the answer or your understanding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you make a move - more context, more depth - on the answer you have.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that builds on the first answer in {{context}}.
_incorrect.final: A good move in {{context}} adds context and depth to the answer you have. Restarting, accepting on tone, or just asking for length do not.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Eight techniques that build understanding
body: Eight ways to use AI to learn, each with a prompt to start it. Select each heading to reveal it.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all eight.

_items.title: Explain it back
_items.body:
Ask the tool to explain an idea, then close it and restate the idea yourself, in your own words, without looking. Comparing your version against the original shows exactly where your understanding breaks down, because the gap only shows up once you try to produce the explanation rather than just recognise it.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Explain} {topic} simply, then wait while I explain it back to you in my own words."
  • "{Summarise} {topic} in three sentences, then ask me to repeat it without looking."
  • "{Break down} {topic} step by step, then tell me which step I get wrong when I explain it back."

_items.title: Socratic questioning
_items.body:
Let the tool question you one step at a time instead of explaining, so you have to produce each answer rather than just recognise it. Reasoning out loud under gentle questioning surfaces exactly where your understanding is thin, because you cannot skip the step you are unsure about.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Act} as a Socratic tutor on {topic}; ask me one question at a time and wait for my answer before the next one."
  • "{Question} me about {topic} one step at a time, and do not give me the answer even if I ask."
  • "{Probe} my understanding of {topic} with follow-up questions until I can explain it clearly."

_items.title: Targeted practice and feedback
_items.body:
Ask for practice matched to your current level, attempt it without help, then ask for feedback on your method rather than just the mark. Separating the attempt from the feedback forces you to commit to an answer first, so the feedback corrects your thinking instead of just confirming what you already suspected.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Set} five questions on {topic} at my level; do not show me the answers until I try each one."
  • "{Create} a short test on {topic}, mark my answers, and tell me what my mistakes say about my method."
  • "{Give} me one hard problem on {topic} and wait until I attempt it before giving feedback."

_items.title: Feedback on your own work
_items.body:
Share a draft and ask a precise question, rather than a vague "is this good", so the feedback is usable. A sharp question about one feature of the work, such as your argument, your structure or your evidence, gets feedback you can act on, where a general request only gets general praise.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Read} my {topic} and tell me what my main argument is; show me where it is unclear."
  • "{Check} this paragraph on {topic} for how well the evidence supports the claim."
  • "{Identify} the weakest point in my argument about {topic} and explain why it is weak."

_items.title: Mapping concepts
_items.body:
Lay out what you already know about a topic, then ask the tool to show how the ideas connect and where the gaps are. Building the map yourself first means the tool fills genuine gaps in your thinking, rather than doing the organising for you.

Try prompts like:

  • "{List} what I understand about {topic} so far; show me how these ideas connect and what I am missing."
  • "{Map} the relationship between these ideas in {topic} and point out any I have left out."
  • "{Organise} my notes on {topic} into a structure and flag where the links are weak."

_items.title: Devil's advocate
_items.body:
State your position on a topic and ask the tool to argue against it, so you can find the weak points in your own reasoning before a marker does. Defending your view against a real counter-argument is a harder test of understanding than simply restating it.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Argue} against this claim about {topic}: give me the strongest counter-arguments I must answer."
  • "{Challenge} my position on {topic} as if you disagreed with it."
  • "{Find} the weakest part of my argument on {topic} and press me on it."

_items.title: Learning through analogy
_items.body:
Ask for an analogy from a field you already know, then ask where the analogy breaks down. The breakdown point is often the most important part of the original idea, because it is exactly where the comparison stops holding.

Try prompts like:

  • "{Explain} {topic} using an everyday analogy, then tell me where the analogy stops working."
  • "{Compare} {topic} to something from a subject I already know, and show me the limits of the comparison."
  • "{Translate} {topic} into a simple analogy, then test whether I can say why it eventually fails."

_items.title: Preparing for reading
_items.body:
Before a difficult chapter or paper, ask for the key terms and debates in plain language, so your first read is productive rather than spent decoding vocabulary. Knowing the terrain in advance means your first pass can focus on the argument instead of the words.

Try prompts like:

  • "{List} the key terms and debates I will meet in this reading on {topic}, in plain language."
  • "{Preview} this chapter on {topic}: what are the main questions it is trying to answer?"
  • "{Flag} any specialist vocabulary in {topic} I should look up before I start reading."

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students prepare the same hard topic for a seminar.

{{learner-a}} asks the tool to summarise the topic and reads the summary twice. It all makes sense on the page. In the seminar, asked to explain the idea without notes, {{learner-a}} cannot do it. The tool had done the understanding, and none of it had moved across.

{{learner-b}} uses two techniques. First, explain it back: {{learner-b}} reads the tool's explanation, closes it, writes the idea from memory, then asks what was missed. Second, a Socratic turn: {{learner-b}} asks the tool to question the explanation one step at a time. The gaps show up, and {{learner-b}} can hold the idea with no tool open.

Both used the same tool on the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} used it to build understanding, not to replace it.

title: Using a technique well
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These checks keep a technique working as learning, not as a shortcut. Try one on your next hard topic.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I pick the technique that fits what I want to understand?
Did I do the thinking, rather than let the tool do it?
Did I explain the idea back in my own words at some point?
Did I let the tool question me, or argue against me?
Did I check my understanding with no tool open?
Did I notice whether my understanding actually grew?

title: Formative check: building understanding
displayTitle: Which use of AI builds your own understanding?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which use of AI builds your own understanding?

_items.text: Have the tool explain an idea, then explain it back in your own words and ask what you missed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Explaining it back makes you do the thinking, so the understanding is yours.

_items.text: Ask the tool for a summary and reread it until it feels familiar.
_items.feedback: Familiar on the page is not the same as understood; you did not do the work.

_items.text: Ask the tool to write the seminar answer for you.
_items.feedback: That hands over the thinking the task was meant to build.

_items.text: Copy the tool's explanation into your notes word for word.
_items.feedback: Copying stores wording, not understanding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining an idea back forces your own thinking, which is how understanding forms.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where you, not the tool, do the thinking.
_incorrect.final: Understanding grows when you do the work, such as explaining the idea back. Summaries, hand-over answers and copying do not build it.

title: Formative check: why it worked
displayTitle: In the worked example, why could the second student explain the idea with no tool open?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why could the second student explain the idea with no tool open?

_items.text: They used techniques that made them do the thinking, such as explaining it back and being questioned.
_items.feedback: Yes. Doing the thinking is what builds understanding you keep.

_items.text: They read the tool's summary more carefully than the first student.
_items.feedback: Careful reading of a summary is still the first student’s approach.

_items.text: They used a tool that gives more detailed summaries.
_items.feedback: A better summary does not do the thinking for you.

_items.text: They memorised the tool's exact wording.
_items.feedback: Memorised wording is not understanding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining back and being questioned build understanding, because you do the work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student did that forced their own thinking.
_incorrect.final: The second student explained the idea back and let the tool question them, so the understanding was theirs. Re-reading, a better tool or memorising would not build it.

title: Formative check: your own topic

_incorrect.final: Understanding a hard idea in {{context}} grows when you explain it back and fix the gaps. Hand-over answers, passive reading, or a simple-sounding summary do not.

displayTitle: When you write a learning prompt, which version is most likely to get a useful answer?

_items.text: One written in the most formal language you can manage.

_items.text: One that states the topic in a single word.

_items.text: One that asks for the longest possible answer.
_items.feedback: Length is not usefulness.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A role, a function and your context make the answer specific.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what gives the tool enough to answer your actual need.

displayTitle: A prompt asks the tool to write your essay on a given title. Why is this a weak learning prompt?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is asking the tool to write your essay a weak learning prompt?

_items.text: It asks the tool to do the task, so it does not help you learn or think.
_items.feedback: Yes. A prompt that offloads the task does nothing for your learning.

_items.text: It is too short for the tool to understand.
_items.feedback: Length is not the problem; the request is.

_items.text: It uses the wrong citation style.
_items.feedback: Style is not the issue here.

_items.text: It does not sound confident enough.
_items.feedback: Confidence is not what a learning prompt needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A prompt that offloads the task does nothing for your learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about who does the thinking when the tool writes the essay.

displayTitle: Your first answer from a tool is clear but too general. What is the best next move?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A first answer is too general. What is the best next move?

_items.text: Make a move on it, such as adding context or asking it to go deeper.
_items.feedback: Yes. A move builds on the answer you already have.

_items.text: Delete it and start a brand-new prompt.
_items.feedback: Restarting loses the dialogue you built.

_items.text: Accept it and move on.
_items.feedback: A general answer left as is does little for you.

_items.text: Ask the same question again, reworded.
_items.feedback: Rewording from scratch resets the dialogue.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A move builds on the answer you already have.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that builds on the first answer.

displayTitle: Which sequence shows prompting used as a dialogue rather than one exchange?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.

_items.text: Ask, then go deeper, add context, check for bias, and verify the claims in turn.
_items.feedback: Yes. Moves made in turn on one dialogue deepen the answer.

_items.text: Ask once and accept whatever comes back.
_items.feedback: One exchange is not a dialogue.

_items.text: Write three unrelated prompts and pick your favourite answer.
_items.feedback: Separate prompts do not build on each other.

_items.text: Ask for the same thing in a more confident tone.
_items.feedback: Tone is not a move; it does not deepen the answer.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Moves made in turn on one dialogue deepen the answer.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where each step builds on the last.

displayTitle: Which use of AI best builds your own understanding of a difficult idea?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.

_items.text: Have the tool explain it, then explain it back in your own words and fix the gaps.

_items.text: Read the tool's summary until it feels familiar.
_items.feedback: Familiarity is not understanding.

_items.text: Ask the tool to answer the question for you.
_items.feedback: That replaces your thinking.

_items.feedback: Copying stores wording, not understanding.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining it back makes you do the thinking, so understanding forms.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where you do the thinking.

displayTitle: You want the tool to find the weak points in your argument. Which technique fits?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which technique finds the weak points in your argument?

_items.text: Ask it to play devil's advocate and give the strongest counter-arguments.
_items.feedback: Yes. Devil’s advocate surfaces the weak points you need to answer.

_items.text: Ask it to rewrite your argument more confidently.
_items.feedback: Rewriting does not test your reasoning.

_items.text: Ask it to agree with your argument.
_items.feedback: Agreement hides the weak points rather than finding them.

title: Orientation
body: You now have three things: a framework for building prompts, a set of moves to deepen a dialogue, and eight techniques for learning. On their own they are separate skills. This lesson joins them into one routine you can keep using, and ties it back to the honest, critical use the earlier courses built.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is not a flawless routine every time. It is to see the framework, the moves and the techniques as one practice, so it carries past this course into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: combine the framework, the moves and the techniques into one deliberate routine
recognise a skilled, critical and honest AI learning routine at work
design your own AI learning routine for {{context}} study beyond this course.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A learning routine is the three strands run as one habit. You frame each prompt with a role, a function and your context. You make moves to deepen the dialogue rather than start again. You choose the technique that fits what you want to understand. Running them together is what makes AI use deliberate.

Two things keep the routine sound, and they come from the earlier courses. Stay critical: test what the tool gives you before you rely on it. And stay honest: do your own thinking and be open about where a tool helped. Skilled prompting without critical, honest use is just faster guessing.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the routine is one pass you run on each task, not four errands. You frame the prompt, deepen it with a move or two, use a technique to build understanding, and stay honest about what you used. Done together, the parts make each other stronger.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about one task in your studies where you will use AI soon. Write the routine you will run: how you will frame the prompt, deepen it, build understanding, and stay honest.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A good AI routine is one habit built from three: the framework, the moves and the techniques. On each task you frame the prompt, deepen the dialogue, choose a technique, and stay critical and honest about what you use. You can now combine the three into a deliberate routine, recognise it at work, and design your own for your studies. This ties skilled prompting to the honest, critical use the earlier courses built.

title: Your routine as one cycle
displayTitle: Your routine as one cycle
body: A good routine runs as a continuing habit, not a one-off. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Frame the prompt
_items.body: Give the tool a role, a clear function and your context, and ask for the method rather than the answer.

_items.title: Deepen the dialogue
_items.body: When the first answer is thin, make a move - expand, add context, go deeper, check bias or verify - instead of starting over.

_items.title: Build understanding
_items.body: Pick a technique such as explaining it back or being questioned, so you do the thinking, not the tool.

_items.title: Check and be honest
_items.body: Test what the tool gives you before you rely on it, be open about how you used it, then run the routine again.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students both plan to use AI across a busy term.

{{learner-a}} has no routine. {{learner-a}} types quick one-line questions, takes the first answer, and never checks it or records how it was used. Some weeks it helps; some weeks it misleads. Because nothing is deliberate, {{learner-a}} cannot tell which is which.

{{learner-b}} works to a routine. Each prompt gets a role, a function and context. When an answer is thin, {{learner-b}} makes a move rather than starting again. For hard ideas {{learner-b}} explains them back or asks to be questioned, checks claims against the reading, and notes any AI use. The practice is skilled, critical and honest at once.

Both used the same tool all term. Only {{learner-b}} had a routine, and so learned more and could defend every step.

displayTitle: Checklist: How to run the routine

instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I frame the prompt with a role, a function and my context?
Did I make a move when the first answer was thin?
Did I use a technique that made me do the thinking?
Did I test what the tool gave me before relying on it?
Was I honest about where and how the tool helped?

displayTitle: Build your AI study routine
title: Build your AI study routine
instruction: Choose a response to see what happens, then follow where it leads. Each choice has consequences.

n1.body: You have two weeks to prepare for an exam and you want AI to help you learn, not just hand you answers. Where do you begin?

_choices.text: Have it generate concise notes on each topic for you to read.
_choices.consequence: Reading AI notes is passive, and the notes may contain errors you would not spot. On its own it is a weak, risky way to learn.

_choices.text: Have it ask you questions and critique your answers.
_choices.consequence: Active retrieval with feedback - one of the strongest ways to learn.

_choices.text: Have it write model answers for you to study from.
_choices.consequence: Model answers can help, but only if you do something active with them.

nNotes.body: You now have a set of AI-written notes and two weeks to go. What do you do with them?

_choices.text: Read and re-read them until the exam.
_choices.consequence: Re-reading feels productive but builds little, and you never checked the notes for errors.

_choices.text: Turn them into questions, test yourself, and check weak spots against your course materials.
_choices.consequence: Now the routine is active and verified - a strong recovery.

nFeedback.body: The AI quizzes you and points out gaps in your answers. How do you treat its feedback?

_choices.text: Accept each correction as right and move on.
_choices.consequence: AI can be confidently wrong. Taking every correction on trust can quietly embed errors.

_choices.text: Check its corrections against your notes or a reliable source, then redo the weak topics.
_choices.consequence: You learn actively and guard against AI error - keep this routine.

nModel.body: You have a set of AI model answers. What do you do next?

_choices.text: Memorise them to reproduce in the exam.
_choices.consequence: Reproducing answers you did not build teaches you little, and leaning on them that heavily edges toward the integrity line.

_choices.text: Compare them with your own attempts to see what you missed, then rewrite in your own words.
_choices.consequence: You use the model as a mirror, not a script - that builds your own understanding.

nGood.body: You built an AI routine that is active - retrieval, feedback, comparison - and checked against reliable materials. That deepens understanding and guards against AI's errors.

nNeutral.body: Active practice is good. But taking AI's corrections on trust can embed its mistakes, so verify its feedback against your own materials or a reliable source.

nPoor.body: Reading or reproducing AI output is passive and risky: it builds little real understanding and can carry errors, or edge toward relying on work that is not your own. Make your AI routine active and checked.

displayTitle: Why run the framework, the moves and the techniques as one routine?
body: Why run the framework, the moves and the techniques as one routine?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why run the framework, the moves and the techniques as one routine?

_items.text: Because each needs the others: you frame a prompt, deepen it, and pick a technique on the same task.

_items.text: Because using all three means you can skip checking the answer.

_items.text: Because one good routine means you never think about AI again.
_items.feedback: A routine is repeated each time, not settled once.

_items.text: Because three separate skills always take longer than one.
_items.feedback: It is not about speed; the strands depend on one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The framework, the moves and the techniques support one another, so they work best as one routine.

title: What makes a prompt strong
displayTitle: What makes a prompt strong
body: A strong prompt names three things. Each one makes the answer more useful.

_items.title: Role
_items.text: Tell the AI who to be, such as a patient tutor or a critical examiner.

_items.title: Function
_items.text: Say exactly what to do, such as explain the method or quiz you on it.

_items.title: Context
_items.text: Give your level, your module and the thing you find hard.

_items.title: The one rule
_items.text: Ask for the method, not the answer, so the thinking stays yours.

title: A prompting session, move by move
displayTitle: A prompting session, move by move
body: A good session is a dialogue, not one question. Open each move to see how it builds on the last.
instruction: Open any move to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Move 1: Open with a framed prompt
_items.body: Set a role, a clear task and your context, then send your first prompt.
_items.advice: In practice: name who the AI should be, what you want it to do, and your level and module. A framed prompt earns a sharper first answer.

_items.title: Move 2: Ask for the method
_items.body: Ask the AI to show the steps or the reasoning, not just the final answer.
_items.advice: In practice: add "show me how to work it out, do not just give the answer". You learn the method, and you can check each step.

_items.title: Move 3: Push back
_items.body: Challenge a weak point, or ask the AI to critique its own answer.
_items.advice: In practice: try "what is the weakest part of that?" or "give me the counter-argument". Pushing back surfaces gaps and deepens the dialogue.

_items.title: Move 4: Apply it yourself
_items.body: Close the tool and redo the task in your own words to check you have learnt it.
_items.advice: In practice: the real test is what you can do with the tool closed. If you cannot, go back a move and work it through again.

title: Order a self-quizzing session
displayTitle: Order a self-quizzing session
body: Self-testing with AI works when you do it in order. Arrange the steps.
instruction: Drag the steps into the right order, then select Submit.

_items.text: Tell the AI your level and the topic you are revising.
Ask it to quiz you with open questions, one at a time.
Answer in your own words before seeing any feedback.
Ask where your answer was weak and why.
Redo the weak points without the AI to confirm you have learnt them.

_feedback.title: A self-quiz that works
_feedback.correct: That is the order. Set the scene, get questioned, answer first, find the gaps, then close them yourself.

_incorrect.final: Not quite. Set up the quiz first, answer before feedback, then act on the gaps last.
_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to come before you can answer, and try again.

title: A routine that keeps the thinking yours
displayTitle: Checklist: A routine that keeps the thinking yours
body: A good routine shares the work with AI without handing over the learning.
instruction: Tick each item once your routine covers it.

_items.text: Have I decided what the AI will do and what I will do myself?
Have I set a point where I close the tool and work alone?
Have I built in a check of anything the AI tells me?
Have I planned to put its guidance into my own words?
Can I say how this routine helps me learn, not just finish faster?
